summary: I checked all 40 references against Crossref, DataCite and arXiv. All 32 DOIs resolve and the 8 arXiv IDs exist, so the bibliography is not fabricated. The literature base, however, is not good enough for an Analytica Chimica Acta methods paper. (1) Two of the three references cited for the motivating soil sample-size claim ([6],[7]) report the opposite of what the sentence says, and one of them was attached through a mislabelled citation key. (2) The most directly relevant prior work in the target journal is missing: Beleites et al. 2013, Anal. Chim. Acta 760:25–33. It predates the cited 'introduction' by Ali et al. and already showed that small-sample learning curves are masked by validation uncertainty, which is this paper's central negative result. (3) The headline identifiability claim ('no pilot, however analysed, can separate ...') is stated without reference to the high-dimensional noise and SNR estimation literature (Dicker 2014; EigenPrism 2017; Verzelen & Gassiat 2018), which shows the limit is one of precision rather than strict non-identifiability when the design covariance is known. (4) Several 'findings' (κ-collapse, noise-driven slope, alignment exponent) are known theoretical results (Patil & Du 2023; Cui et al. 2022; Caponnetto & De Vito 2007) and are not attributed. (5) The Results and discussion contains no citations at all. Further gaps: uncited standard sample-size guidance (ASTM E1655, ISO 12099), uncited conformal and multiple-testing methods, missing data references, arXiv preprints cited where published versions exist, and Crossref metadata errors copied into the reference list without correction.
strengths: Every DOI (32) resolves on Crossref or DataCite and every arXiv ID (8) exists; authors, titles, volumes and pages match the registry records apart from the formatting errors listed in R8-C01-11. No fabricated references were found.

Most citations support their sentences: the random-matrix ridge-risk references [15–18], the spectral-bias and task-alignment references [19–22], the IPL learning-curve sources [8–10], the Tecator origin [33], SNV [34], Kennard–Stone [38] and the Bayesian bootstrap [28].
References are numbered in order of first citation, as Elsevier's numbered style requires, and every reference is cited in the text.

issues.title: Refs [6] and [7] do not support the claim they are cited for, and the reference behind [6] was swapped in by DOI
issues.description: Introduction: 'Empirical studies in soil spectroscopy show that accuracy keeps improving well beyond a few hundred samples before levelling off [5–7]'. Only [5] (Ng et al. 2020) supports this. Both [6] and [7] are farm- or local-scale studies with about 200 samples in total, so they cannot show improvement 'well beyond a few hundred samples'. Both conclude the opposite: accuracy levels off at a few tens to about a hundred samples. The bibliography pipeline shows how this happened. The key used for [6] is 'kuang2014', and the authors' literature matrix describes it as 'Kuang & Mouazen (2014, Geoderma)'. No such paper exists. The DOI attached to that key belongs to Debaene et al. 2014, a different study. The relevant Kuang & Mouazen paper is Eur. J. Soil Sci. 63 (2012) 421–429. So the citation was checked for DOI validity, not for whether it supports the claim.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 22 (Introduction, '[5–7]'). Reference [7] (Lucà et al., Geoderma 288 (2017) 175–183), per its abstract: 216 samples from a 33-ha forest; the full-set accuracy was matched with 29 (PCR), 72 (SVMR) and about 115–130 (PLSR) calibration samples. Reference [6] (Debaene et al., Geoderma 214–215 (2014) 114–125, DOI 10.1016/j.geoderma.2013.09.022 checked on Crossref): about 200 samples at one Polish experimental station; satisfactory SOC/clay predictions with about 79 calibration samples, with K-means selection recommended. Reference [5] (Ng et al., SOIL 6 (2020) 565–578), per the Crossref abstract: 350 to about 7650 samples; 'accuracy increased with an increasing number of training samples', with PLSR/Cubist hypothesised to plateau. manuscript/refs/verify_refs.py: 'kuang2014': '10.1016/j.geoderma.2013.09.022'. supplementary/LITERATURE_MATRIX_AND_NOVELTY_MAP.md row 'Ng et al. (2020, SOIL); Kuang & Mouazen (2014, Geoderma)'. EXPERIMENT_LOG.md line 18: Lucà et al. was added late as an 'additional verified reference'.
issues.corrective_action: Rewrite the sentence so that each claim matches its source. For example: 'In local and farm-scale soil studies, accuracy levelled off at a few tens to about a hundred samples [6,7,Kuang & Mouazen 2012], whereas in large libraries it kept improving into the thousands [5]'. This contrast is itself useful for the paper because it fits the shallow 8.3%-per-doubling slopes in Section 4.2. Fix the citation key and the Supplementary literature matrix. Re-check every citation for whether it supports its claim, not only for DOI validity.

issues.title: Closest prior art in the target journal is missing (Beleites et al. 2013, ACA), which makes the priority statement wrong and anticipates a central negative result
issues.description: The Introduction says learning-curve sample-size planning was 'introduced to analytical chemistry for Raman classification by Ali et al. [8]'. Five years earlier the same Jena group published 'Sample size planning for classification models' in Analytica Chimica Acta (Beleites, Neugebauer, Bocklitz, Krafft, Popp, Anal. Chim. Acta 760 (2013) 25–33, doi:10.1016/j.aca.2012.11.007). It discusses learning curves for small spectroscopic data sets and concludes that 'the learning curve can be completely masked by the random testing uncertainty due to the equally limited test sample size' (PubMed 23265730 abstract). That is essentially this manuscript's main negative finding: the slope per doubling is smaller than the sampling error of a small pilot's own CV estimate, so FLAT is hard to beat and the n needed for a target error cannot be forecast (Sections 4.3 and 4.5). The paper is in the target journal, is directly on topic and shares authors with [8]. Editors and referees will expect it to be cited and discussed. Without it, the paper overstates both the novelty of its 'ill-conditioning' argument and the priority of [8].
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 24 ('introduced to analytical chemistry for Raman classification by Ali et al. [8]'); line 214 ('With slopes of about 8.3% per doubling, a factor-two error in n corresponds to a smaller change in RMSE than the sampling error of a small pilot's own cross-validated RMSE'); line 198 (FLAT not significantly different from RPM). Neither the reference list (lines 306–384) nor the Supplementary literature matrix mentions Beleites et al. 2013. Crossref confirms the DOI and metadata.
issues.corrective_action: Cite Beleites et al. 2013 in the Introduction as the first learning-curve sample-size planning work in analytical chemistry, and correct the priority statement about [8]. In Section 4.5 and the Conclusions, say that the masking of the learning curve by validation uncertainty was shown earlier for classification. Present the present contribution as quantifying the same effect for regression calibration across 38 tasks and explaining it mechanistically through the noise floor.

issues.title: The absolute non-identifiability claim ignores, and partly conflicts with, the literature on estimating noise variance and signal-to-noise ratio in high dimensions
issues.description: Section 2.4 states: 'No pilot, however analysed, can separate target power hidden in weak modes from irreducible noise without such an assumption [a parametric form of s_k]'. The Highlights, Section 4.4, Limitation 2 and the Conclusions repeat this as a central result ('the noise floor, which pilot sets cannot identify'). No reference supports it, and the established literature says something more qualified. (a) With Gaussian design, EigenPrism (Janson, Barber, Candès, JRSS-B 79 (2017) 1037–1065) gives valid confidence intervals for the signal ℓ2-norm and the noise level with p > n, without sparsity assumptions or knowledge of the noise level (Crossref abstract). (b) Dicker (Biometrika 101 (2014) 269–284) gives method-of-moments estimators of σ² and the signal strength with known design covariance and no assumption on the form of β. (c) Verzelen & Gassiat (Bernoulli 24 (2018) 3683–3710) give minimax rates and show that 'the knowledge of the design distribution is shown to play a critical role'. Consistent estimation is possible in much wider regimes when the design distribution is known. That is exactly RPM's situation, because Σ is estimated from cheap unlabelled spectra. So the limit is one of statistical precision, which grows with p/n0, not a strict non-identifiability that holds 'however analysed'. Section 4.4 and the ablations show only that RPM-T and free-r fits fail. They do not show that no estimator can work.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 82 (Section 2.4, 'No pilot, however analysed, can separate...'); line 206 (Section 4.4); line 274 (Limitation 2); line 281 (Conclusions: 'a pilot of 25–200 samples cannot reveal how much of its residual error is learnable signal'); Highlights.docx bullet 3. The reference list cites no work on noise-variance or SNR estimation. Crossref checks: 10.1111/rssb.12203 (EigenPrism), 10.1093/biomet/ast065 (Dicker 2014), 10.3150/17-bej975 (Verzelen & Gassiat 2018).
issues.corrective_action: Cite and discuss this literature. Recast the claim as a precision or minimax limit at the studied p/n0 (p = 94–216, n0 = 25–200), for example by stating the expected standard error of a moment estimator of σ²/var(y) at these sizes. Alternatively, keep the 'however analysed' wording only if it is backed by the experiment below. Soften the matching Highlight and Conclusions sentences accordingly.
issues.proposed_experiment: Evaluate an assumption-light noise-level estimator on the existing pilots: a Dicker (2014) moment estimator or EigenPrism, whitened with the pool covariance (unlabelled spectra). Report its error for σ²/var(y) against the large-sample fit and, optionally, use it to fix σ² in RPM. This directly tests whether a pilot 'however analysed' can identify the noise floor. It is cheap: closed form, existing pilots, no new data.

issues.title: Results and discussion, Limitations and Conclusions contain no citations; findings are not compared with prior literature
issues.description: Section 4 is titled 'Results and discussion', but Sections 4.1–4.10, Section 5 and Section 6 contain no bracketed citations at all. I counted every citation in manuscript lines 138–282 and found zero. All 40 references are cited in Sections 1–3 only. Several findings need comparison with published evidence. The 8.3%-per-doubling slope and the levelling off should be set against soil sample-size studies [5–7] and Kuang & Mouazen 2012. The higher alignment exponent for MIR than for VisNIR, and the chemical explanation offered, should be set against the OSSL paper [29], whose abstract reports MIR models are more accurate than VisNIR/NIR, and against MIR/VisNIR reviews. The Kennard–Stone pilot bias should be set against the representative-sampling literature, including Kennard–Stone [38] itself and Ramirez-Lopez et al. 2014. The mango season-shift result should be set against Anderson et al. [31], a paper specifically about robustness across seasons. The noise-floor result needs the theory references in issue R8-C01-05. Uncited assertions in the Discussion include 'The inverse-power-law extrapolation currently used in analytical chemistry' (Section 4.3) and the chemical interpretation of r ('broad, overlapping overtone and combination bands and strong scattering leave the chemical information in subtle shape differences'; Section 4.2).
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md: grep over lines 138–282 finds no '[n]' citations; citations occur only on lines 22–131. Uncited claims at line 166 (spectroscopic interpretation of r), line 170 (slope and noise floor), line 176 ('currently used in analytical chemistry'), line 259 (Kennard–Stone, season shift) and line 281 ('power-law extrapolation used today').
issues.corrective_action: Add explicit comparison with prior work for each main finding. Support the spectroscopic interpretation in Section 4.2 with NIR/MIR band-assignment and soil-spectroscopy references, for example Pasquini, Anal. Chim. Acta 1026 (2018) 8–36, plus a MIR-versus-VisNIR soil comparison. Cite [31] and the representative-sampling literature in Section 4.8. ACA readers expect the Results and Discussion to place results in the literature.

issues.title: Several claimed findings are known theoretical results and need attribution: κ-equivalence, source condition, noise-driven slope crossover, non-asymptotic validity
issues.description: Contribution (i) and three of the five Highlights present as empirical discoveries several statements that follow from, or were predicted by, existing theory that is not cited. (a) The κ-collapse ('test errors measured at different calibration sizes and penalties collapse onto a single function of the effective regularisation') is the structural/risk equivalence along paths in the (penalty, aspect-ratio) plane proved by Patil & Du ('Generalized equivalences between subsampling and ridge regularization', arXiv:2305.18496, NeurIPS 2023). That work also gives a data-dependent method to determine the equivalent paths, which is very close to RPM's mapping of the pilot's path onto κ. (b) The alignment exponent s_k ∝ λ_k^r is the classical source condition (Caponnetto & De Vito, Found. Comput. Math. 7 (2007) 331–368). With the eigen-decay it forms the source/capacity framework used throughout [19–22]. (c) The finding that the slope is 'governed mainly by the irreducible-noise fraction' is the noiseless-to-noisy crossover of learning-curve exponents characterised by Cui, Loureiro, Krzakala & Zdeborová (J. Stat. Mech. 2022, 114004), who also show it on real data. (d) Eqs. (2)–(3) are applied at n0 = 25 with p up to 216, far from the proportional asymptotics of [15,16]. The non-asymptotic, dimension-free deterministic equivalent of Cheng & Montanari (Ann. Statist. 52 (2024) 2879–2912) is the appropriate justification, and the much older learning-curve approximations of Sollich & Halees (Neural Comput. 14 (2002) 1393–1428) are part of the lineage. (e) GCV for ridge is Golub, Heath & Wahba (Technometrics 21 (1979) 215–223), not only the spline paper [23]. Omitting (a) also weakens the novelty statement 'To our knowledge, the theory has not been turned into a forecasting tool'. That statement needs to be positioned against data-driven equivalence-path estimation and against work using the eigen-spectrum to explain scaling laws ([25]; Simon et al., the eigenlearning framework, which is listed in the authors' own literature matrix but not cited).
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 28 (contribution i), line 160 (κ-collapse presented as a direct test), lines 166–170 (alignment exponent and noise floor), line 26 ('To our knowledge...'), line 44 (Eq. 2 attributed only to [15,16,18]). Highlights.docx bullets 1–3. Supplementary Note 3 lists Simon et al. (arXiv:2110.03922) but the main text does not cite it. All suggested DOIs and arXiv IDs were checked: 10.1214/24-aos2449, 10.1007/s10208-006-0196-8, 10.1088/1742-5468/ac9829, 10.1162/089976602753712990, 10.1080/00401706.1979.10489751, arXiv 2305.18496.
issues.corrective_action: Cite (a)–(e) in Sections 1, 2.2 and 4.1–4.2. Present the κ-collapse and the noise-floor dependence as the first empirical confirmation of known theory on spectroscopic calibrations, not as discoveries. Rename or define r explicitly as a source-condition exponent. Narrow the novelty sentence to what is actually new: non-omniscient forecasting to larger n from a pilot plus unlabelled spectra, evaluated on 38 tasks.

issues.title: Claims about 'current practice' rest on one classification paper; standard sample-size guidance for NIR/MIR calibration is described but not cited
issues.description: The Abstract ('current learning-curve extrapolation assumes a power-law shape'), Significance ('Power-law extrapolation ... should be abandoned'), Section 4.3 ('The inverse-power-law extrapolation currently used in analytical chemistry (IPL3)'), the Conclusions ('the power-law extrapolation used today') and the cover letter all present IPL extrapolation as established practice for quantitative calibration. The only support is a single Raman classification paper [8], plus [9,10] from microarray and NLP classification. These fitted IPLs to classification accuracy or error rate, not to the RMSE of a regression. IPL3 as specified in Section 3.5 (within-pilot curve at 25–85%, weighted fit to RMSE) is therefore the authors' adaptation, not 'the' current method. Conversely, the guidance practitioners actually use is mentioned but not cited: 'Current guidance is largely heuristic, for example minimum sample numbers expressed relative to model complexity, or experience from related applications'. Examples are the minimum calibration-set sizes in ASTM E1655 (Standard Practices for Infrared Multivariate Quantitative Analysis), ISO 12099 (NIR in feed and cereals), and Shenk & Westerhaus, Crop Sci. 31 (1991) 469–474. A recent survey of learning-curve use for decisions in ML (Mohr & van Rijn, Mach. Learn. 113 (2024) 8371–8425) is also missing.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 11 (Abstract Background), line 15 (Significance), line 22 (uncited heuristic guidance), line 106 (IPL3 'as used by Ali et al. [8]'), line 176, line 281; cover_letter.docx ('The learning-curve extrapolation currently used for this purpose in analytical chemistry fits an assumed power-law shape').
issues.corrective_action: Cite the standards and the classical guidance (ASTM E1655, ISO 12099, Shenk & Westerhaus 1991) where heuristic guidance is mentioned. Rephrase 'currently used in analytical chemistry' as 'proposed for sample-size planning in analytical chemistry [8, Beleites 2013]'. State that IPL3 is the authors' adaptation of classification-based IPL planning to regression RMSE. Tone down 'should be abandoned' to a statement about IPL extrapolation from small pilots as specified here.

issues.title: Competing domain approaches to calibration-set size and representativeness are omitted, including one that uses unlabelled spectra
issues.description: The paper argues that 'unlabelled spectra are cheap, so the covariance spectrum can be estimated accurately long before many reference values exist' and lists use of unlabelled spectra as a distinguishing element in the novelty map. Soil spectroscopy already has a method that sets the calibration-set size from unlabelled spectra: Ramirez-Lopez et al., 'Sampling optimal calibration sets in soil infrared spectroscopy', Geoderma 226–227 (2014) 140–150. It chooses the size by comparing the spectral (principal-component) distributions of candidate subsets with the whole library. Kuang & Mouazen (Eur. J. Soil Sci. 63 (2012) 421–429) studied the number of samples needed at farm scale and appears in the authors' own matrix under a wrong year and journal. Both bear on the sample-size decision analysis (Section 4.5) and on the Kennard–Stone and representativeness discussion (Section 4.8). Riley-type minimum-sample-size criteria [3,4] are cited but never used as a baseline or compared numerically, even though [4] applies them to chemometric regression with continuous outcomes.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 26 ('unlabelled spectra are cheap...'), lines 100 and 214 (decision metric), line 259 (Kennard–Stone pilots), line 22 ([3,4] cited only in passing). supplementary/LITERATURE_MATRIX_AND_NOVELTY_MAP.md novelty map ('unlabelled spectra for the spectrum'). Crossref confirms 10.1016/j.geoderma.2014.02.002 and 10.1111/j.1365-2389.2012.01456.x.
issues.corrective_action: Discuss Ramirez-Lopez et al. 2014 and Kuang & Mouazen 2012 in the Introduction and in Sections 4.5 and 4.8. Make clear that RPM uses unlabelled spectra for a different purpose: the eigen-spectrum for error extrapolation, not representativeness. Optionally report the Riley/Konstantinidis minimum n for the tasks next to the decision results, so readers can see how those criteria compare with the observed curves.
issues.proposed_experiment: Optional and cheap: compute the Riley/Konstantinidis minimum sample size (continuous-outcome criteria) for each task from the pilot's R² and effective df, and tabulate it against the ground-truth curves. This uses existing outputs only.

issues.title: Methods taken from the statistics literature are used without citation, and NIR-specific interval work listed in the authors' own matrix is not cited
issues.description: These method components have no reference. Split-conformal calibration of the bands (Section 3.6, 'split-conformal calibration across data sets'; Section 4.5, which supports a headline claim of the Abstract): cite Vovk et al. 2005 and Lei et al., JASA 113 (2018) 1094–1111, and note that calibrating across data sets requires exchangeability across sources, which the conformal literature treats explicitly. Holm correction (Holm, Scand. J. Stat. 6 (1979) 65–70). The DF-OLS formula ŝ²{1+1/n+df/(n−df−1)}, which is the classical random-design prediction-error formula (e.g., Breiman & Freedman, JASA 78 (1983) 131–136). Type-II maximum likelihood. The bootstrap confidence intervals. The delta-method intervals for IPL3. In addition, Bouckaert et al., 'A comparison of methods for estimating prediction intervals in NIR spectroscopy: Size matters', Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst. 109 (2011) 139–145, deals directly with how interval quality in NIR depends on training size. It appears in the authors' literature matrix and in verify_refs.py but is not cited, nor is the group-conformal NIR interval paper (Talanta, doi:10.1016/j.talanta.2026.130941) that the matrix lists as prior art.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 111 (DF-OLS), line 117 (type-II ML), line 125 (split-conformal), line 131 (Holm, bootstrap), line 106 (delta method), line 210 (calibrated-band results). manuscript/refs/verify_refs.py lists 'bouckaert2011', 'faber1997' and 'talanta2026', but none appears in the reference list (lines 306–384). Crossref confirms 10.1080/01621459.2017.1307116, 10.1016/j.chemolab.2011.08.008 and 10.1080/01621459.1983.10477941.
issues.corrective_action: Add the method citations listed above. Cite Bouckaert et al. 2011 and the NIR conformal-interval work in Section 4.5. State the exchangeability assumption behind leave-one-source-out conformal calibration and cite its source.

issues.title: Data sets are missing from the reference list, and the dataset provenance cited is incomplete or inconsistent
issues.description: Elsevier asks authors to cite underlying datasets as data references in the reference list. These data sources have no reference entry: the SWRI diesel NIR set, the IDRC 2002 shoot-out tablets, the CGL mixture set (its original publication is not given anywhere), Tecator in the OpenML version 505 actually used (only the 1992 paper [33] is cited), the OSSL v1.3 data release itself (the Data availability statement says only 'OSSL public bucket', with no URL, version DOI or access date), and the ICRAF-ISRIC, AfSIS-1 and NeoSpectra libraries. [30] (Sanderman et al. 2020) is cited for 'KSSL MIR and VisNIR', but it covers MIR only. The mango dataset is cited as version 6 ([32], doi:10.17632/46htwnp833.6, DataCite issued 2026-02-15), while the Data availability statement gives the unversioned concept DOI (doi:10.17632/46htwnp833). Readers cannot tell which version produced the reported 4021 fruits.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 88 (Section 3.1 data sources), line 293 (Data availability), references [29], [30], [32], [33]. DataCite record for 10.17632/46htwnp833.6: publicationYear 2026, relation IsVersionOf 10.17632/46htwnp833.
issues.corrective_action: Add a data reference with version, URL or DOI, access date and licence for each source. Cite the original publications for the diesel, shoot-out, CGL, ICRAF-ISRIC, AfSIS and NeoSpectra data. Cite a KSSL VisNIR source in addition to [30]. Use the same versioned mango DOI in [32] and in the Data availability statement.

issues.title: arXiv versions are cited for papers that now have peer-reviewed versions; one substantive claim rests on an unrefereed preprint
issues.description: Five references point to arXiv although the papers have been formally published. [12] Adriaensen et al. appeared in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2023), doi:10.52202/075280-0872. [18] Atanasov et al. appeared in J. Stat. Mech. (2026) 043404, doi:10.1088/1742-5468/ae4bba (per the arXiv journal_ref; confirmed on Crossref), and it is cited as a source for Eq. (2). [19] Bordelon et al. appeared in Proc. ICML 2020, PMLR 119:1024–1034. [24] Jacot et al. appeared in NeurIPS 33 (2020). [25] Wei et al. appeared in Proc. ICML 2022, PMLR 162. [4] (Konstantinidis et al., arXiv 2510.01210, submitted 2025-09-17, no journal reference) is the only support for 'have only recently been transferred to chemometrics'. That is acceptable but should be labelled as a preprint.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md reference list lines 312, 328, 340, 342, 352, 354. arXiv API: journal_ref fields for 2002.02561 and 2405.00592; Crossref record 10.1088/1742-5468/ae4bba (J. Stat. Mech. 2026, issue 4, 043404); Crossref record 10.52202/075280-0872 (NeurIPS 36).
issues.corrective_action: Replace the arXiv citations with the published versions, including DOIs or proceedings volumes and pages. Keep [4], [13] and [14] as preprints, marked '(preprint)'.

issues.title: Metadata errors in the reference list and non-compliance with ACA's Elsevier numbered style
issues.description: Errors carried over unedited from Crossref metadata: [26] 'l. E. Frank' should be 'I.E. Frank' (Ildiko Frank; Crossref has the OCR string 'lldiko'). [22] has a stray asterisk in the title ('...teacher-student model*'). [37] has double punctuation ('Procedures.,'). [5] gives 'W. d. S. Mendes' instead of 'W. de S. Mendes'. [3] lacks the volume (BMJ 368 (2020) m441). [39] gives the page as '80' instead of 80–83. Style: the ACA Guide's Elsevier numbered format is 'J. Sci. Commun. 163 (2010) 51–59', with abbreviated journal titles, no comma after the year and an en dash in page ranges. The manuscript uses full journal titles, '(2001), 109-130' with a comma and a hyphen, and inconsistent author formats: full given names in [12–14,18,19,24,25], initials elsewhere. The AI-use declaration says the authors 'verified every reference against Crossref, DataCite or arXiv'. The errors above, and the mismatch between claim and source in R8-C01-01, show that the check was an automated DOI lookup without curation.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md lines 310, 314, 348, 356, 378, 382 (specific errors); lines 306–384 (style); line 297 (AI declaration). Checked against Crossref records for all 32 DOI-bearing references: all DOIs resolve, and titles, volumes and pages otherwise match.
issues.corrective_action: Correct the listed entries. Reformat all references to the ACA/Elsevier numbered style with ISO-abbreviated journal titles and author initials. Revise the AI declaration to describe accurately what was verified (DOI resolution and metadata) and what the authors checked manually (claim support).

issues.title: Supplementary Note 3 (literature matrix) cites works missing from every reference list, misdescribes one, and contains internal project-management text
issues.description: The Supplementary literature matrix and novelty map cite Kuang & Mouazen (2014, Geoderma), which does not exist as cited (see R8-C01-01). They also cite Bouckaert et al. 2011, Faber & Kowalski 1997, Simon et al. 2021 and a Talanta 2026 paper by DOI only. None of these is in the main reference list, and the Supplement has no reference list of its own. The note says 'All references were verified ... (manuscript/refs/verified_refs.json)', which points to an internal file path. Section 4, 'Topic-selection record', contains internal project-management content ('standard-free calibration transfer — crowded in ACA 2026', 'Toxicology/hazard-prediction topics were excluded by design'). This content does not belong in journal Supplementary Material and does not support any claim in the paper.
issues.corrective_action: Either remove Supplementary Note 3 or turn it into a properly referenced related-work table that uses the main reference numbering. Correct the Kuang & Mouazen entry to Eur. J. Soil Sci. 63 (2012) 421–429. Delete the topic-selection record and the internal file path.

issues.title: Some citations only weakly support the sentences they are attached to
issues.description: [1] (a PLS tutorial) and [2] (a validation tutorial) are cited for multivariate calibration being 'the workhorse of rapid quantitative analysis in agriculture, food, fuels, pharmaceuticals and soil science'. Neither documents that breadth of application. An NIR review would, for example Pasquini, Anal. Chim. Acta 1026 (2018) 8–36. [27] (Hoerl & Kennard 1970, which introduced ridge) is cited for ridge, PCR and PLS being 'closely related shrinkage estimators'. That paper predates PLS and does not discuss the relationship; [26] alone supports the claim. [35] (Kapoor & Narayanan, a general taxonomy of ML leakage) is the only citation for grouped cross-validation with whole groups left out. The standard methodological reference for grouped or blocked CV is Roberts et al., Ecography 40 (2017) 913–929.
issues.evidence: manuscript/build/manuscript_full.md line 22 ('[1,2]'), line 26 ('[26,27]'), line 92 ('[35]'). Crossref checked: 10.1016/j.aca.2018.04.004 and 10.1111/ecog.02881.
issues.corrective_action: Replace or supplement these citations with sources that directly support each statement, as suggested above.

recommendation_rationale: Counts by severity: FATAL 0, CRITICAL 0, MAJOR 5, MODERATE 4, MINOR 4. None of the literature problems invalidates the experiments, so rejection is not warranted on citation grounds. However, the framing of the contribution depends on priority and novelty statements that the literature does not support: the priority of [8] given Beleites 2013, absolute non-identifiability given Dicker, EigenPrism and Verzelen & Gassiat, and κ-collapse and noise-floor 'findings' that existing theory already predicts. The paper also misattributes an introductory claim to [6,7] and engages with no literature at all in its Results and discussion. Fixing this means rewriting the Introduction, Section 2.4, the Discussion, the Highlights and the Conclusions, plus one cheap optional experiment (a moment or EigenPrism noise-level estimator on the existing pilots). That is a major revision.
